claim: MWAA operates Dulles and Reagan National under a federal lease from the U.S. DOT that began in 1987 and, after successive extensions, now runs to 2100 — making the FAA/DOT simultaneously landlord, safety regulator, and grant-maker.
source_title: Secretary of Transportation and Airports Authority Sign Lease Extension for Operation of Washington's Airports
supporting_excerpt: extension of thirty years to the current 50-year lease the Airports Authority holds with the federal government to manage and improve Ronald Reagan Washington National and Washington Dulles International Airports; original 1987 lease, later extended, expiring in 2100
caveat: Exact current expiration (2067 vs 2100) reported inconsistently across sources; 2024 extension cited as pushing expiration to 2100.

claim: MWAA's board has 17 members: 7 appointed by the Virginia governor, 4 by the D.C. mayor, 3 by the Maryland governor, and 3 by the President of the United States.
supporting_excerpt: Governor of Virginia appoints seven Members; Mayor of the District of Columbia appoints four Members; Governor of Maryland appoints three Members; President of the United States appoints three Members with advice and consent of the U.S. Senate.
caveat: Composition set by 2011-2012 reform; presidential appointees require Senate confirmation.

claim: MWAA airport-system revenue bonds carry AA- (S&P), AA- (Fitch), and Aa3 (Moody's) with stable outlooks; Fitch cited dual-hub resilience, balanced carrier mix, and capital-program progression.
supporting_excerpt: airport system revenue bonds received AA- from Fitch and S&P Global, and Aa3 from Moody's, all with stable outlooks; Fitch noted resilience of complementary dual-large-hub system, well-balanced system-wide carrier mix, capital program progression.
caveat: Ratings apply to the airport-system credit, separate from Dulles Corridor Enterprise (Toll Road/Metrorail) debt.

claim: In 2018 MWAA sold Digital Realty a 424-acre parcel adjacent to Dulles for $236.5 million, and MWAA staff proposed devoting proceeds to reducing the costs airlines pay to operate at Dulles.
supporting_excerpt: Digital Realty acquired the 424 acre parcel in September 2018 for $236.5 million from MWAA. MWAA staff proposed the proceeds of the sale be devoted to reducing costs that airlines pay to do business at Dulles.
caveat: Corroborated by Bisnow reporting; that parcel was not described as within a runway approach/departure surface.

claim: MWAA is preparing to unveil a $20B+ Dulles expansion to roughly 90 million annual passengers (about triple current levels), which the Trump administration prodded it to accelerate and with which United Airlines concurred.
source_title: MWAA almost ready to unveil Dulles expansion plan sought by Trump
supporting_excerpt: modernization to accommodate 90 million annual passengers, more than triple current levels; federal officials prodded MWAA to accelerate; estimates range to over $20 billion; United Airlines central and concurred.
caveat: Plan not yet formally adopted at time of reporting; no new runway mentioned.

claim: FAA thermal-exhaust-plume guidance treats vertical plume velocities above 4.3 m/s as a potential hazard to aircraft operations near airports.
source_title: Technical Guidance Assessment Tool — Thermal Exhaust Plume Impact
supporting_excerpt: Plume velocities in excess of 4.3 m/s are considered a potential hazard to aircraft operations.
caveat: Threshold applies to vertical velocity at evaluated altitude; hazard conditions worst in calm winds/low temps/stable stratification.

claim: FAA revenue-use and land-release rules require airport-generated revenue to be reinvested in the airport, and permit release of federally-obligated land only where the release benefits the airport and creates no incompatible land use; non-aviation community interest does not count as an airport benefit.
supporting_excerpt: revenue produced by leasing/other revenue-producing activity of airport property be reinvested in the airport; a release cannot create incompatible land-uses or interfere with current or future aeronautical activities; non-aviation interest does not constitute an airport benefit.
caveat: Grant Assurance 25 (revenue) supplements assurances 19-22 and 29 cited by the planner; 49 USC 47107/47133 statutory basis.

claim: Washington Dulles is a hybrid-residual airport whose airline use agreement splits net remaining revenues via a defined revenue-sharing formula, so non-aeronautical revenue partly reduces airline costs.
supporting_excerpt: Washington Dulles has a bilateral large-hub airline use agreement and is classified as a hybrid residual airport; net remaining revenues are split per a defined revenue-sharing formula in the Airline Agreement.
caveat: Secondary characterization; exact revenue-sharing math and MII terms not disclosed in cited source.

claim: The United Airlines long-term lease at Dulles was extended through 2024, placing the use-and-lease renegotiation window in the current period.
source_title: Airports Authority and United Airlines Execute Long-Term Lease at Dulles International
supporting_excerpt: seven-year extension of a lease previously set to expire at end of 2017, extending through 2024.
caveat: Any subsequent extension beyond 2024 not confirmed in cited sources; renegotiation status inferred.

claim: Dulles cost-per-enplanement peaked at $26.47 in 2013 and was kept below $20 only with state grant money and transfers from Reagan National; industry commentary projected it could rise sharply under continued capital spending.
source_title: It May Be a Mistake For United to Grow Dulles
supporting_excerpt: cost per enplanement peaked at $26.47 in 2013; only after Virginia grant money and transfers from National did Dulles get CPE back below $20; without subsidies CPE could reach $90.64 by 2035.
caveat: $90.64/2035 is a projection under stated assumptions, not an official MWAA forecast.

claim: Northern Virginia data-center land values reached roughly $3M+/acre, with a November 2025 Loudoun sale exceeding $6M/acre, illustrating the one-time land rent the parcel could capture.
source_title: Data Center Sale Sets New Loudoun Price Record
supporting_excerpt: November 2025 sale of 97 acres east of Leesburg for $615 million set a record, first transaction exceeding $6 million per acre; land values had surged past $3 million per acre from about $500,000 in 2017.
caveat: Market comparables, not an MWAA appraisal of the specific parcel.

claim: Data centers face organized local political opposition in Northern Virginia, including Prince William County's rejection of a large (~2,000-acre) data-center rezoning amid community outcry.
source_title: Prince William County Board of Supervisors rejects plans for 2,000-acre data center
supporting_excerpt: Prince William County Board of Supervisors rejects plans for 2,000-acre data center amid community protest.
caveat: Different jurisdiction than MWAA land; illustrates regional political headwind, not a direct MWAA precedent.
